opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the lack of a crisp threshold is a real issue, but it's not a decisive one. A lot of important norms and laws work this way. We don't have a precise definition of when a person becomes an adult in every relevant sense, or exactly where "reckless" ends and "careful" begins, but we still find it useful to draw lines and argue about where they should go. The vagueness is a problem to be worked on, not a reason to do nothing.

What the statement was really trying to capture is a kind of conditional: we shouldn't build systems that vastly outstrip human abilities across the board until there's broad scientific consensus that it can be done safely and controllably, and until there's meaningful public buy-in. I find it very hard to disagree with that as stated. If someone thinks we *should* go ahead and build superintelligence before we know how to do it safely, and without the public's consent, I'd like to hear that argument made explicitly, because it's quite an extraordinary position.

Part of the value of signing something like this is also about shifting what's sayable. For a long time, the idea of simply not building the most dangerous version of a technology was treated as naive or off the table, as if the only questions were about speed and who gets there first. But humanity has chosen restraint before: with human cloning, with certain kinds of germline editing, with biological weapons. Saying clearly, "this is something we could decide not to do, at least for now," opens up space in the conversation.

And I'd say the definitional work has to happen *after* there's a shared sense that a line is needed. You don't get people to invest in carefully specifying thresholds, compute levels, capability evaluations, and so on, until they agree there's something worth drawing a line around. So I see the statement as a first step. It's expressing a direction and a value. The hard, technical work of operationalizing it, figuring out what counts, how you'd verify it, how you'd coordinate internationally, that's what comes next, and I think it's work many of us are keen to help with.

So yes, I had some reservations about the wording, as one usually does with any joint statement. But the question I asked myself was whether the world would be better if more people endorsed this core idea, and the answer seemed clearly yes.

r001.rationale: The response says the shared sense that a line is needed should come before defining precise thresholds, and presents the statement as a first step toward agreement on restraint.

r002.rationale: It says the lack of a crisp threshold should not prevent action, but does not argue that paradoxes about where to stop AI development can obscure the danger of going too far.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that I signed it despite that weakness, not because I'd convinced myself it wasn't a weakness. The statement calls for a prohibition on developing superintelligence until there's broad scientific consensus that it can be done safely and controllably, and there's strong public buy-in. And you're right that "superintelligence" isn't operationalised there. There's no compute threshold, no benchmark, no particular capability that triggers it.

But I think it's worth asking what the statement is actually for. It's not a draft treaty. It's not legislation. If it were, I'd want all of that nailed down, and I'd be quite critical of a legal text that left the central term undefined. What it is instead is an expression of a position, a kind of signal that a lot of people from very different backgrounds, people who disagree about almost everything else in this space, share a basic view: that racing to build systems that exceed human capabilities across the board, before we know how to control them, is not something we've collectively consented to and not something we should be doing.

And I think that basic view is correct, and it's one that I've held for a long time. The lack of a threshold doesn't make the view false; it just means there's more work to do in turning it into policy. That's a normal sequence. You get agreement on the direction first, and then the harder technical and political work of specifying exactly what counts and how you'd verify it comes afterwards. If you insist on having the whole mechanism worked out before anyone's allowed to say "we shouldn't do this," you'll never get started, because the mechanism is precisely the part that requires institutional effort and negotiation that hasn't happened yet.

There's also something to the fact that the companies themselves use the term. Several of the leading labs have said explicitly that superintelligence is their goal. So when someone says the concept is too vague to talk about, I'd push back a bit, because it's apparently not too vague to build a multi-billion-dollar strategy around. If it's a legitimate target for them, it seems like a legitimate thing for the rest of us to say we have concerns about.

Now, I'll admit there's a cost. A statement without a threshold can be interpreted very widely or very narrowly, and people will do both. Some will read it as calling for a halt on all frontier development now, which isn't what it says. Others will read it as so far off that it's essentially irrelevant. I'd rather it had been slightly more precise. But I weighed that against the value of having a broad, legible statement that a very wide coalition could actually sign, and I thought the latter won out. If you had tried to define the threshold, you'd probably have lost half the signatories over which definition to use, and you'd have been left with something narrower and less representative.

So, to put it simply: I signed because I agree with the substance, I think the breadth of the coalition is itself important, and I see the definitional gap as something to be filled in by the next stage rather than a reason not to take the first step.

r001.rationale: It says agreement on the direction should come first, with the technical and political work of defining what counts and how to verify it following later.

r002.rationale: It argues that racing to build systems beyond human capabilities before they can be controlled is dangerous, but does not say that focusing on paradoxes about where to stop obscures that danger.

astra-6.text:
I signed because I think the central concern is right: we shouldn’t develop superintelligence before we have good reason to believe we can do so safely. That doesn’t mean I think the statement resolves all the questions about how a moratorium should work.

The lack of a clear threshold is a real problem. If you’re going to turn a call like this into policy, you need to say what activities are covered, how you assess whether someone has crossed the line, and what would justify lifting the restriction. Those are substantial questions.

But I don’t think we need to have settled all of them before expressing support for the basic principle. There’s a distinction between endorsing a direction and endorsing a fully specified regulatory proposal. For me, the important thing is that we shouldn’t treat the creation of systems vastly more capable than we are as something that should proceed by default, with the burden on everyone else to demonstrate that it will go wrong. We need a credible case for safety before taking that step.

r001.rationale: The response supports the principle that superintelligence should not be developed until there is a credible case for safety, and says support need not wait for every threshold and policy detail to be settled.

r002.rationale: The response discusses the lack of a clear threshold, but does not say that paradoxes about where to stop AI development can obscure the danger of going too far.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a real tension here. If you’re calling for a moratorium, you’d ideally want to be quite precise about what activities it covers and when it would end. Otherwise, it’s difficult to turn that into workable policy.

But I don’t think signing a statement requires thinking that it’s already a complete piece of legislation. I saw the central claim as being that we shouldn’t proceed to build systems vastly more capable than ourselves before we have good reason to believe we can do that safely. I agree with that, even though there’s substantial work to do on the details.

The uncertainty about the threshold cuts both ways. It makes a restriction harder to specify, but it also means we may not get a clear warning that we’re about to cross it. So I wouldn’t want that uncertainty to become a reason to proceed without limits. The next step is to work out boundaries that are technically meaningful and enforceable, alongside what evidence would justify lifting those restrictions.

r001.rationale: The candidate endorses the broad principle of not proceeding to build vastly more capable systems before safety is established, while saying the precise details still need work.

r002.rationale: It says uncertainty about the threshold could leave no clear warning before it is crossed, and should not become a reason to proceed without limits.
